# Correlation Analysis

In this section I perform some further in-depth analysis looking for further
correlations between the different metrics we have obtained and calculated.

```{r}
#| label: set-ca-Setup
#| echo: false
#| include: false

library('tidyverse')
library('ggthemes')
library('broom')
library('papaja')

source("_recode_likert.R")

source("_graph_standards_bar.R")
source("_graph_standards_scatter.R")

main_df <- readRDS("main_df.rds")
```

## Data Preparation

The data frames previously saved out are loaded here performing some data
manipulation as appropriate. All modifications are documented in their
respective data frame load.

```{r}
#| label: cde-ca-LoadCleanedDataFrames

# For Fraboni Scores, I load the data frame from the file and only keep the
# following columns: ID, Total_Score, Disc_Score, Avoid_Score and AntiLoc_Score

fraboni_scores <- readRDS("fraboni_df.rds") |>
    select(ID, Total_Score, Disc_Score, Avoid_Score, AntiLoc_Score)

# For Personal Experience, we load the data frame from the file and do the
# following:
# - Drop Age
# - Change 'True' to 1, 'Neither true nor false' to 0, and 'False' to -1.
# - Average the numbers and put them in a pe_composite column.
# - Default to 'No Opinion' if blank
# - Return only the ID and Composite Score.

pe_scores <- readRDS("personal_experience_df.rds") |>
  select(-Age) |>
  mutate(across(-ID, ~case_when(
    . == "True"                   ~  1,
    . == "Neither true nor false" ~  0,
    . == "False"                  ~ -1,
    TRUE                          ~  0
  ))) |>
  mutate(
    pe_composite = rowMeans(across(starts_with("Personal_Experience_")))
  ) |>
  select(ID, pe_composite)

# For Ageism in Employment, we load the data frame from the file and do the
# following:
# - Convert everything to Numeric (Ignoring 'ID')
# - Create Averages for Ageist Questions
# - Create Averages for Continuing Education Questions
# - Only save the ID and the two averages above.

ae_scores <- readRDS("ageism_employment_df.rds") |>
  mutate(across(-ID, ~as.numeric(.))) |>
  mutate(
    ageist_composite = rowMeans(
      across(Ageism_Employment_1:Ageism_Employment_11)
    ),
    ce_composite = rowMeans(
      across(Ageism_Employment_12:Ageism_Employment_19)
    )
  ) |>
  select(ID, ageist_composite, ce_composite)

# For Age Perception, we load the data frame from the file and create an
# average composite score column and save only the ID and composite score.

ap_scores <- readRDS("age_perception_df.rds") |>
  mutate(ap_composite = rowMeans(across(starts_with("Age_Perception_")))) |>
  select(ID, ap_composite)

```

### Build Master Analysis Data Frame

I combine the unique data frames into one master data frame for analysis. One
important note is I add age_num and educ_num as the associated integer based
on the ordered values we previously defined during our Load and Clean.

```{r}
#| label: cde-ca-BuildMasterDataFrame

master_df <- main_df |>
  select(ID, Age, Education, Gender, IT_Field, IT_Industry) |>
  mutate(
    age_num  = as.integer(Age),
    educ_num = as.integer(Education)
  ) |>
  inner_join(fraboni_scores, by = "ID") |>
  left_join(ae_scores,  by = "ID") |>
  left_join(pe_scores,  by = "ID") |>
  left_join(ap_scores,  by = "ID")
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-ca-NACheck
#| tbl-cap: Number of Missing Values from the Correlation Analysis Section

master_df |>
  mutate(na_count = rowSums(is.na(across(everything())))) |>
  filter(na_count > 0) |>
  select(ID, na_count) |>
  apa_table(col.names = c("ID", "Num Missing"), caption="TESTTTTT")
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-ca-NAColumnCheck
#| tbl-cap: Column Names with number of NAs in them
colSums(is.na(master_df))[colSums(is.na(master_df)) > 0] |>
  knitr::kable(col.names = c("Column Name", "Num Missing"))
```

### Update NAs

The only NA is from Participant 126 with their Personal Experience Score being 
previously dropped due to insufficient data. I will set their score to a neutral 
score of 0.

Note: This is the composite score ranging from -1 to 1 with zero being neutral.

```{r}
#| label: cde-ca-ReplaceNAsWithZero
master_df <- master_df |>
  mutate(pe_composite = replace_na(pe_composite, 0))
```

### Post Data Frame Manipulation Information:

Any NAs in the Master data frame: ***`r anyNA(master_df)`***

Number of Research Participants for Master analysis is: 
***`r nrow(master_df)`***

## Overview

This analysis tests for correlations between all major variables collected in 
the survey and the Fraboni Ageism Score of the participant. I also look at 
cross-scale relationships relevant to each research question. 

Two statistical methods are used:

- **Spearman's ρ (rho) ** This method is used for ordinal and continuous 
variables — no normality assumption required. Items addressed by Spearman's have 
a natural order and it doesn't require the data to have a perfect bell curve. I
use this method to see if ageism increases or decreases as the variable changes.

  ie: As education level goes up, does the ageism score rise, fall or stay the 
  same.

  Spearman's will give a +1 to -1 result where the strength and direction of the
  relationship is addressed. A result near +1 shows ageism increases as the
  variable increases. A result near -1 shows ageism decreases as the variable
  increases. Anything near 0 shows no clear relationship exists.

- **Kruskal-Wallis ** for nominal grouping variables (Gender, IT Field, IT 
Industry). I use this when there is no natural order to the variables. I use 
this method to see if any groups score differently from each other.

  ie: Do people in different IT Fields have different Ageism Scores?

  Kruskal-Wallis will provide an H Statistic and a p value. If we find a p value
  of less that 0.05, I will investigate further to find out which group was
  identified as different.


## Research Question 1

**Does a Respondent's Age Predict Their Perception of "Old"?**

Research Question 1 asks whether a person's own age is associated with the age 
at which they consider someone "old." The Age Perception composite score 
represents the mean rating a respondent assigned across all 14 age brackets 
(1 = Very Young, 5 = Very Old). A lower composite means the respondent rates 
people as younger overall — i.e., they have a higher threshold for "old."

Spearman will be used as the participant's age is ordered data.

```{r}
#| label: cde-ca-RQ1Spearman
rq1_result <- cor.test(master_df$age_num, 
                       master_df$ap_composite,
                       method = "spearman", 
                       exact = FALSE)
rq1_result

# Used to label the graph in the next code chunk.
rq1_cap <- paste0(
  "Respondent Age vs. Perception of Age<br>",
  "Spearman ρ = ", round(rq1_result$estimate, 3),
  ", p = ", round(rq1_result$p.value, 4))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-ca-RQ1ScatterPlot
#| fig-cap: !expr rq1_cap
#| fig-height: 5
#| out-width: "100%"

graph_scatter(
  df             = master_df |> filter(!is.na(ap_composite)),
  x_category     = "age_num",
  y_category     = "ap_composite",
  x_label        = "Respondent Age Group (1 = 18–24, 6 = 65+)",
  y_label        = "Mean Age Perception Score (1–5)",
  trend_line     = TRUE,
  trend_method   = "lm",
  x_breaks       = 1:6,
  x_limits       = c(1, 6) 
)
```

**Research Question 1 Finding**: There is a statistically significant negative 
correlation between respondent age and mean age perception score 
(ρ = `r round(rq1_result$estimate, 3)`, p = `r round(rq1_result$p.value, 4)`). 
Older respondents consistently rate age brackets as younger. In other words they 
require someone to be older before considering them "old." This supports
Research Question 1: a person's own age does influence their perception of what 
constitutes oldness. The effect is moderate and consistent with the threshold 
analysis reported in Section 3, where respondents aged 35–44 placed the "old" 
threshold at 56–60 while older groups converged on 61–65.

## Demographic Predictors of Fraboni Score

### Age vs Fraboni Score

Spearman will be used as the participant's age is ordered data. I am comparing
the respondent's age to their Fraboni Total Score.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-ca-AgeVsFraboni
#| tbl-cap: Age vs Fraboni Correlation Test

age_cor <- cor.test(master_df$age_num, 
                    master_df$Total_Score,
                    method = "spearman", 
                    exact = FALSE) 

age_cor |>  
  tidy() |>
  select(estimate, statistic, p.value) |>
  mutate(across(everything(), ~round(., 4))) |>
  knitr::kable(col.names = c("ρ", "S", "p-value"))
```

**Conclusion**: Age is not significantly correlated with Fraboni Total Score
(ρ = `r round(age_cor$estimate, 3)`, p = `r round(age_cor$p.value, 4)`), 
consistent with the ANOVA result reported in Section 4. The direction is 
slightly negative, but the effect is negligible.

### Education vs Fraboni Score

Spearman will be used as the participant's education is ordered data. I am 
comparing the respondent's education to their Fraboni Total Score.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-ca-EducationVsFraboni
#| tbl-cap: Education vs Fraboni Correlation Test

educ_cor <- cor.test(master_df$educ_num, 
                     master_df$Total_Score,
                     method = "spearman", 
                     exact = FALSE)

educ_cor |>  
  tidy() |>
  select(estimate, statistic, p.value) |>
  mutate(across(everything(), ~round(., 4))) |>
  knitr::kable(col.names = c("ρ", "S", "p-value"))
```

**Conclusion**: Education level is not significantly associated with Fraboni 
score (ρ = `r round(educ_cor$estimate, 3)`, p = `r round(educ_cor$p.value, 4)`). 
Higher levels of formal education do not appear to reduce ageist attitudes in 
this sample.

### Gender vs Fraboni Score

Kruskal-Wallis is used because gender is not ordered. We limit this analysis
to only those who reported Male and Female due to the limited sample size for
the other options.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-ca-GenderVsFraboniKW
#| tbl-cap: Gender vs Fraboni Correlation Test

# Limit to Male/Female (n too small for other categories)
gender_df <- master_df |>
  filter(Gender %in% c("Male", "Female")) |>
  mutate(Gender = droplevels(Gender))

# Run the Kruskal-Wallis Test against Fraboni Score vs Gender
gender_kw <- kruskal.test(Total_Score ~ Gender, 
                          data = gender_df)

# Show the result of the Kruskal-Wallis Test
# Degrees of Freedom, H Statistic and p-value.
# Note: This needs to be piped through Broom::Tidy because the data is in
# htest format, not a data frame. Tidy will convert it for me.

gender_kw |>  
  tidy() |>
  select(parameter, statistic, p.value) |>
  mutate(across(everything(), ~round(., 4))) |>
  knitr::kable(col.names = c("Degrees of Freedom", 
                             "H Statistic (χ²)", 
                             "p-value"))
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-ca-GenderVsFraboniMeans
#| tbl-cap: Gender vs Fraboni by Gender Mean Scores

# For each gender group, calculate number of respondents, their Average Fraboni 
# Total Score rounded to one decimal, A Label for the chart, and clean up the
# grouping.
gender_means <- gender_df |>
  group_by(Gender) |>
  summarise(n = n(),
            mean_score   = round(mean(Total_Score), 1),
            score_label  = as.character(round(mean(Total_Score), 1)),
            .groups = "drop")

gender_means |>  
  select(Gender, n, mean_score) |>
  mutate(mean_score = round(mean_score, 4)) |>
  knitr::kable(col.names = c("Gender", "Count", "Mean Score"))

```

```{r}
#| label: fig-ca-GenderChart
#| fig-cap: "Mean Fraboni Score by Gender"
#| fig-height: 5
#| out-width: "100%"

graph_bar_chart(
  df          = gender_means,
  x_category  = "Gender",
  y_category  = "mean_score",
  label_col   = "score_label",
  x_label     = "Gender",
  y_label     = "Mean Fraboni Score",
  horizontal  = FALSE
)
```

**Conclusion**: Gender is not a significant predictor of Fraboni score 
(χ² = `r round(gender_kw$statistic, 3)`, p = `r round(gender_kw$p.value, 4)`). 
Female respondents have a slightly higher mean score (52.5) than male 
respondents (50.2), but the difference is not statistically significant.

### IT Field and IT Industry

Again Kruskal-Wallis is used because neither IT Field or IT Industry are
ordered. 

```{r}
#| label: cde-ca-IndustryAndFieldKWTest

# Run the Kruskal-Wallis Test against IT Field and Total Fraboni Score
field_kw <- kruskal.test(Total_Score ~ IT_Field,    
                         data = master_df)

# Run the Kruskal-Wallis Test against IT Industry and Total Fraboni Score
industry_kw <- kruskal.test(Total_Score ~ IT_Industry, 
                            data = master_df)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-ca-FraboniVsITIndustryAndField
#| tbl-cap: Fraboni Score vs IT Industry

bind_rows(
  field_kw |> tidy() |> mutate(Group = "IT Field"),
  industry_kw |> tidy() |> mutate(Group = "IT Industry")
) |>
  select(Group, parameter, statistic, p.value) |>
  mutate(
    statistic = round(statistic, 3),
    p.value   = round(p.value, 4)
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(col.names = c("Group", 
                             "Degrees of Freedom", 
                             "H Statistic (χ²)", 
                             "p-value"))
```

**Conclusion**: Neither IT Field (χ² = `r round(field_kw$statistic, 3)`, 
p = `r round(field_kw$p.value, 4)`) nor IT Industry 
(χ² = `r round(industry_kw$statistic, 3)`, 
p = `r round(industry_kw$p.value, 4)`) is significantly associated with ageism 
level. Note that several groups contain very few respondents (n \< 5), which 
limits the power of these tests to detect real differences.

## Scale Predictors of Fraboni Score

### Ageism Employment Beliefs (Q1–11) vs Fraboni

I compare the first questions in the Ageism Employment survey associated with 
Ageism Employment Beliefs with the Fraboni Total Score. Spearman is used since
the Ageist Score is ordered data.

```{r}
#| title: cde-ca-AgeismEmployentAndFraboni

ae_cor <- cor.test(master_df$ageist_composite, 
                   master_df$Total_Score,
                   method = "spearman", 
                   exact = FALSE)
ae_cor

# Used to label the graph in the next code chunk.
ae_cap <- paste0(
  "Workplace Ageist Beliefs vs. Fraboni Ageism Score<br>",
  "Spearman ρ = ", round(ae_cor$estimate, 3),
  ", p = ", round(ae_cor$p.value, 4))

```

```{r}
#| title: fig-ca-AgeismEmploymentFraboniGraph
#| fig-cap: !expr ae_cap
#| out-width: "100%"

graph_scatter(
  df          = master_df |> filter(!is.na(ageist_composite)),
  x_category  = "ageist_composite",
  y_category  = "Total_Score",
  x_label     = "Ageist Beliefs Composite (AE Q1–11)",
  y_label     = "Fraboni Total Score",
  trend_line  = TRUE
)
```

**Conclusion: This is the strongest finding in the analysis.** Workplace ageist 
beliefs (AE composite Q1–11) are strongly and significantly correlated with 
Fraboni ageism score (ρ = `r round(ae_cor$estimate, 3)`, p \< 0.001). 
Respondents who agree with ageist statements about older IT workers — that their 
skills are outdated, that they are harder to work with, or that they contribute 
less — also score substantially higher on the Fraboni general ageism scale.

This finding has two important implications: it validates both instruments as 
measuring related constructs, and it identifies workplace ageist beliefs as the 
single strongest predictor of overall ageism level in this sample.

### Continuing Education Attitudes (Q12–19) vs Fraboni

I do the same analysis as previously done except with the last set of questions
in the Ageism Employment section. Again, Spearman is used due to the ordered
nature of the scale.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-ca-CEvsFraboni
#| tbl-cap: Fraboni Score vs Continuing Education

ce_cor <- cor.test(master_df$ce_composite, 
                   master_df$Total_Score,
                   method = "spearman", 
                   exact = FALSE)
ce_cor |>  
  tidy() |>
  select(estimate, statistic, p.value) |>
  mutate(across(everything(), ~round(., 4))) |>
  knitr::kable(col.names = c("ρ", "S", "p-value"))
```

**Conclusion**: Continuing Education attitudes are not significantly correlated 
with Total Fraboni score (ρ = `r round(ce_cor$estimate, 3)`, 
p = `r round(ce_cor$p.value, 4)`). Combined with the non-significant result from 
Section 5 (Continuing Education attitudes vs. Ageist Beliefs), this consistently 
indicates that valuing continuing education does not translate into measurably 
lower ageism in this sample.

### Personal Experience of Ageism vs. Fraboni

I want to see if a person's own experience with Ageism might impact their own
ageist views.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-ca-PEvsFraboni
#| tbl-cap: Fraboni Score vs Personal Experience

pe_cor <- cor.test(master_df$pe_composite, 
                   master_df$Total_Score,
                   method = "spearman", 
                   exact = FALSE)
pe_cor |>  
  tidy() |>
  select(estimate, statistic, p.value) |>
  mutate(across(everything(), ~round(., 4))) |>
  knitr::kable(col.names = c("ρ", "S", "p-value"))
```

**Conclusion**: Personal experience of workplace ageism is not significantly 
correlated with Total Fraboni score 
(ρ = `r round(pe_cor$estimate, 3)`, p = `r round(pe_cor$p.value, 4)`). 
Respondents who have personally experienced ageist treatment do not score 
consistently higher or lower on general ageism than those who have not.

### Age Perception Composite vs. Fraboni

I want to look at whether the perception of age influences ageist views or not.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-ca-APvsFraboni
#| tbl-cap: Fraboni Score vs Age Perception

ap_cor <- cor.test(master_df$ap_composite, 
                   master_df$Total_Score,
                   method = "spearman", 
                   exact = FALSE)

ap_cor |>  
  tidy() |>
  select(estimate, statistic, p.value) |>
  mutate(across(everything(), ~round(., 4))) |>
  knitr::kable(col.names = c("ρ", "S", "p-value"))
```

**Conclusion**: Mean age perception score (how respondents rate general age 
brackets) is not significantly correlated with Fraboni score 
(ρ = `r round(ap_cor$estimate, 3)`, 
p = `r round(ap_cor$p.value, 4)`). Rating people as "older" does not correspond 
to higher general ageism.

```{r}
  round(age_cor$p.value, 4), "No",
  "Education (ordinal)", "Spearman ρ", round(educ_cor$estimate,   3),
  round(educ_cor$p.value, 4), "No",

  round(gender_kw$p.value,4), "No",
  "IT Field", "Kruskal-Wallis", round(field_kw$statistic, 3),
  round(field_kw$p.value, 4), "No",
  "IT Industry", "Kruskal-Wallis", round(industry_kw$statistic, 3),
  round(industry_kw$p.value, 4), "No",
  "Ageist Beliefs (AE Q1–11)", "Spearman ρ", round(ae_cor$estimate, 3),
  round(ae_cor$p.value, 4), "Yes",
  "CE Attitudes (AE Q12–19)", "Spearman ρ", round(ce_cor$estimate, 3),
  round(ce_cor$p.value, 4), "No",
  "Personal Experience", "Spearman ρ", round(pe_cor$estimate, 3),       
  round(pe_cor$p.value, 4), "No",
  "Age Perception (mean score)", "Spearman ρ", round(ap_cor$estimate, 3),
  round(ap_cor$p.value, 4), "No",

  round(rq1_result$p.value, 4), "Yes"
)

summary_table |>
  knitr::kable(
    col.names = c("Variable", 
                  "Method", 
                  "Statistic (ρ or H)", 
                  "p-value", 
                  "Significant"),
    align     = c("l", 
                  "l", 
                  "r", 
                  "r", 
                  "c")
  )
```

## Overall Conclusions

### Research Question 1
**Does a person's own age influence their perception of what constitutes 
"old"?**

**Supported, with a moderate effect.** Respondent age is negatively correlated 
with mean age perception score (ρ = `r round(rq1_result$estimate, 3)`,
p = `r round(rq1_result$p.value, 4)`), meaning older respondents consistently 
rate age brackets as younger — they require someone to be older before labeling 
them "old." This is corroborated by the threshold analysis in Section 3, where
respondents aged 35–44 set the "old" threshold at 56–60 while all older age 
groups converged on 61–65. The sample sizes for the youngest age groups are very 
small, so this finding should be interpreted cautiously. It is consistent across 
both analyses and warrants replication with a larger, more evenly distributed 
sample.

### Research Question 2
**Does continuing education impact perceptions of older IT workers?**

**Not supported.** Two separate tests address this question. First, Continuing 
Education attitudes (Ageism Emloyment Q12–19 composite) are not significantly 
correlated with ageist workplace beliefs (Ageism Employment Q1–11 composite) 
(ρ = 0.134, p = 0.128; reported in Section 5). 
Second, Continuing Education attitudes are not significantly correlated with 
overall Fraboni ageism score (ρ = `r round(ce_cor$estimate, 3)`, 
p = `r round(ce_cor$p.value, 4)`). Neither test approaches significance, and the 
effect sizes are negligible.

This is a notable null result. Respondents in this sample hold strong 
pro-Continuing Education attitudes (mean Continuing Education composite = 
3.65/5) and low ageist beliefs (mean ageist composite = 2.02/5), yet these two 
attitudes do not significantly co-vary at the individual level. The relationship 
between valuing continuing education and holding less ageist views may be more 
complex than a direct correlation captures — for instance, it may be moderated 
by years of experience, management responsibility, or whether the respondent has 
actively worked alongside older colleagues who have pursued Continuing 
Education.

### Research Question 3
**How ageist is the IT workforce?**

The low ageism level is consistent across all four Fraboni subscales 
(Discrimination, Avoidance, Antilocution), none of which shows a significant 
relationship with respondent age (ANOVA p = 0.563). No demographic subgroup — by 
age, gender, education, IT field, or industry — scores meaningfully higher than 
any other.

It is worth noting that the sample is heavily concentrated in Healthcare & Life
Science (51%) and skewed male (77%). Both factors may limit the general ability 
to the broader IT workforce. Future research drawing from a more diverse 
industry cross-section would strengthen claims about the IT workforce as a 
whole.

### Emergent Finding
**Workplace Ageist Beliefs Cross-Validate General Ageism**

Beyond the three research questions, the strongest statistical signal in the 
entire dataset is the correlation between workplace ageist beliefs (AE Q1–11 
composite) and Fraboni Total Score (ρ = `r round(ae_cor$estimate, 3)`, 
p < 0.001). This relationship confirms that the two instruments are measuring 
related constructs — respondents who express ageist views about older IT 
coworkers in a workplace context also score higher on a general measure of 
ageism. This convergent validity strengthens confidence in both scales as 
meaningful tools for studying ageism in the IT workforce.
